newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition demands democracy, free press.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition demands democracy, free press.

text.p: Serbian opposition supporters held a massive rally in Belgrade on Sunday to commemorate the anniversary of pro-democracy riots six years ago.

"A lot has happened in these six years, but one thing remains the same - Serbia is still at a crossroads - either we opt for progress or continued life with those we've been saddled with for the past fifty years," opposition leader and Belgrade mayor Zoran Djindjic told about 30,000 supporters.

Djindjic, Vuk Draskovic and Vesna Pesic led an opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition campaign for three months of daily protests against election fraud in the biggest challenge yet to Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's autocratic rule.
The demonstrations ended in February when Milosevic restored their November local election victories in 14 Serbian cities, including Belgrade, which his ruling Socialists had annulled.
Zajedno then called off the streets protests, but pressure has been kept up for freedom of the press, a crucial issue ahead of parliamentary and presidential elections expected this year.
Milosevic's Socialists, fighting to reinstate their battered popularity, are loath to concede control over broadcast media.
The West, outraged by the election fraud and fearing more violence in the Balkans, has pressed Milosevic to free the media and open a dialogue with the opposition.
Zajedno said on Sunday it would attend round table talks with the Socialists only if decisions were reached by consensus, or two-thirds majority, and if covered live by television.
It suggested talks start on March 20 and discuss freedom and openness of the state media and a balanced approach to political parties, particularly in the election campaign.
The round table discussion would also draft a law on the funding of political parties as well as new election rules.
"Serbia has taken the first and irreversible step towards democracy...it is an unstoppable process," Djindjic said.
The process was launched six years ago when thousands battled with the police in Belgrade.
Two people were killed, scores were injured and arrested. Milosevic sent in his tanks to quell the unrest.
Today the Sociallists are in desperate need of capital to kick-start an economy starved of investment and hard currency.

Experts have dismissed Milosevic's efforts at privatisation as a publicity stunt because he lacks the funds to push it through and his party diehards seem unwilling to implement Western-style reforms.
The United States has been instrumental in barring Belgrade from financial institutions until Serbia shows a commitment to democracy and human rights.
